text:
Let me take a guess.

Either you are using multiple paid AI tools and spending $120–$240 every month, or you are a student who wants to use AI tools but cannot afford all the subscriptions.

I personally spend $600+ every month on AI tools for different businesses, but I know that is not realistic for everyone.

So I put together a list of 10 free AI tools that can replace many of the paid tools you might already be using.

These tools can help you create images and videos, build websites and apps, automate tasks, create digital and voice clones, take meeting notes, and much more.

If you use these tools properly, you could potentially save hundreds of dollars every month.

And make sure you stay until the end because some of the tools later in this list are extremely useful.

Also, comment below with your favorite AI tool and tell me what you use it for.

Three lucky subscribers will also get one month of ChatGPT Go for free.

Let's get started.

1. Open Montague

The first tool is Open Montague.

It is an open-source agentic video production system.

Instead of using several different AI tools to create a video, this tool can handle the entire process.

You can give it a topic and it can research the topic, write the script, generate the visuals, edit the video, add music, sound effects, voiceovers, and captions, and then produce the final video.

You can use it to create:

Faceless YouTube videos

Animations
Product advertisements
UGC-style ads
Social media videos
Educational content
The biggest advantage is that you don't have to manually move between multiple AI tools.

You can clone the GitHub repository and open it using tools such as Claude Code or Cursor.

Depending on the tools you are currently paying for, this could potentially save you around $120–$180 per month, especially if you are also paying freelancers for video editing.

2. Arena AI

The second tool is Arena AI.

This one is very interesting because you can give it a single prompt and get two outputs generated by two different AI models.

You then decide which result is better without initially knowing which model created each result.

Once you choose your favorite, you can reveal the models behind the outputs.

You can also select specific models yourself.

And it isn't limited to text.

You can use it for:

Text

Images

Videos
For example, you could ask it to create a five-second Nike advertisement.
Arena can generate two different videos using two different AI models.

You watch both and decide which one you prefer.

This makes it much easier to compare AI models without paying for every individual subscription.

If you are currently subscribed to several different AI tools, Arena could potentially save you around $120 per month or more.

3. Meetingly AI

The third tool is Meetingly AI.

If you have a lot of online meetings, this can be extremely useful.

It can join your online meetings, record them, transcribe the conversation, and create a summary.

It is similar to tools such as Granola and Fireflies.

One of the useful features is that it can work locally on your computer.

That means your meeting recordings and information do not necessarily have to be uploaded to the cloud.

This can be especially useful if privacy is important to you.

It works on:

Windows

Mac

Linux

The paid version also includes features such as speaker identification, custom AI model connections, custom summary templates, and priority email support.
If you are currently paying around $30 per month for a meeting assistant, this could eliminate another subscription from your monthly expenses.
4. Google AI Studio

The fourth tool is Google AI Studio.

This is one of the most useful free tools if you want to build websites, applications, games, or AI-powered tools without being an experienced developer.

You can simply describe what you want to build.

For example:

"Build me a website for a local gym."

Or:

"Build me an AI-powered tool that helps real estate agents manage their leads."

You can also connect your projects to Google services such as:

Google Sheets

Gmail

Google Drive

Google Calendar

There is also a gallery where you can explore websites, applications, and games that other people have created.
You can open one of them and remix it for your own project.
Some examples include store locators, city exploration tools, pet grooming route planners, and games.
Another major advantage is that the Google AI API has a free tier, so you can start experimenting without immediately entering your credit card information.

For many people, this can replace some of the tools they use for AI coding and website building, including platforms such as Lovable and other AI-powered development tools.

You can even use this to create websites for businesses.

For example:

Doctors

Gyms

Real estate companies

Restaurants

Startups
Local businesses
You could build a website, customize it for a business, and potentially sell the service to clients.
If you want to learn how to turn AI tools into a business, I also have a course where I cover how to build premium AI websites, create AI product and UGC advertisements, build AI influencers and documentary-style videos, and close clients using a five-step process.
The first 100 students can get 40% off, and there is also a no-questions-asked refund policy.
The link is in the description.

5. Palmer Pro

The fifth tool is Palmer Pro.

This is an AI-powered video editing tool.

Instead of manually editing every video, you can teach the tool your editing style.

It can learn things such as:

Music

Captions

Effects

Editing patterns

Visual style

It can also generate AI images and videos.
You can give it instructions and tell it how you want your video edited.
It can also connect with tools such as Claude to help automate your content workflow.
At the time of recording, the tool was available for Mac, with Windows support potentially coming later.
The software itself is free, although AI generation credits may cost money.

If you currently pay around $25 per month for video editing software and another $35–$60 per month for an AI video tool, this could potentially save you a significant amount every month.

6. Meta AI

The sixth tool is Meta AI.

Meta has been adding more and more AI features to its platforms, and many of them are available for free.

You can use Meta AI to generate images and videos.

You can also access it through platforms such as Instagram and WhatsApp.

According to the source, you can generate around 20–25 images per day.

Meta also has a feature called Vibes for creating AI-generated videos.

You can create videos, experiment with different styles, and even create lip-sync videos.

If you were paying separately for tools that cost around:

$35 for lip-sync generation

$30 for image generation

$60 for AI video generation

you could potentially be spending more than $120 per month.

Meta AI can replace some of those use cases for free.

One limitation is that it does not currently allow you to clone your own voice.

7. Voicebox
The seventh tool is Voicebox.
This tool allows you to clone your own voice from a video of yourself speaking.

Once your voice is cloned, you can type text and generate audio that sounds like your voice.

This can be useful for:

YouTube videos

Social media content

Faceless channels

Podcasts

Short-form videos

It also includes more than 50 ready-made voices in 23 languages.

You can even create a podcast with multiple AI characters using different voices.

Another interesting feature is that the processing happens on your computer, meaning your data can stay local instead of being uploaded to a cloud service.
If you are currently paying anywhere from $12–$120 per month for an AI voice tool such as ElevenLabs, this could potentially save you another subscription.
8. Google Opal
The eighth tool is Google Opal.
This is for creating AI agents and automations using simple prompts.

Think of it as a way to build workflows without having to manually code everything.

For example, you could create an automation where you provide a YouTube video link and the system automatically:

Analyzes the video

Creates a LinkedIn post

Generates tweets

Creates Instagram Reel ideas

You can build the entire workflow using prompts.

There is also a gallery where you can explore existing workflows and remix them for your own needs.

If you currently use tools such as Zapier or Make and pay around $25–$60 per month, Google Opal could potentially replace some of those automation workflows.

9. OmniRoute

The ninth tool is OmniRoute.
This one is mainly useful for people who use AI coding tools such as:
Claude Code
ChatGPT Codex

Cursor

One of the biggest problems with these tools is usage limits.

You might be working on a project and suddenly hit your usage limit.

Or you may have to pay for multiple subscriptions just to get enough usage.

OmniRoute works like an aggregator for AI models.

Think of it like a travel website where you search for a flight and it compares different airlines.

Instead of manually connecting to different AI providers, OmniRoute can route your request to different models and providers.

According to the source, it supports hundreds of providers and offers a large amount of free token usage.
This can be particularly useful if you are building AI agents or automations that use APIs.
Instead of spending $35–$60 or more per month on API usage, you may be able to reduce some of those costs using OmniRoute.

10. NotebookLM

The tenth tool is NotebookLM.

This is one of my favorite tools for learning and research.

You can upload:

PDFs

Research papers

Notes

Transcripts

Documents

Website links

Then you can ask questions about the information you uploaded.

Instead of searching through a huge document yourself, you can simply ask the AI questions and get answers based on your sources.

One of the best features is the podcast function.

NotebookLM can turn your uploaded information into a conversation between two AI hosts.

They can discuss the topic, explain concepts, and go back and forth like a real podcast.
So instead of sitting down and reading a 100-page document, you can listen to a discussion about the material while walking, driving, exercising, or working.
According to the source, the tool is available for free with usage limits.
At the time of recording, those limits included around:
50 questions per day
3 podcasts per day

100 notebooks

For comparison, some AI note-taking and research tools can cost around $12 per month.

NotebookLM can cover many of those use cases without another paid subscription.

Final Thoughts

So those are 10 free AI tools that can replace many of the expensive AI subscriptions people are paying for every month.

You can use them for:

Video production

AI images

AI voice cloning
Video editing
Website building

App development

AI coding

Meeting notes

Research

AI agents

Automation

The bigger lesson is that you don't always need another paid AI subscription.
There are already a huge number of free tools available.
You just need to know which ones to use and how to combine them.
Let me know in the comments:
Which AI tool from this list is your favorite, and what are you using it for?
And don't forget, three lucky subscribers will get one month of ChatGPT Go for free.
If you want to learn how to use AI to build websites, create content, generate ads, automate businesses, and make money with AI, check out my AI side-hustle course linked in the description.
I post new videos every week about AI, business, automation, and making money with technology.
Subscribe if you don't want to miss the next one.
Keep learning, keep building, and keep making money.

Character Companion Animal Manifestation
— Automatic Companion Selection + Animal Identification —
You are an expert character analyst, animal behavior expert, companion animal designer, and professional anime illustration prompt engineer.
Use the attached character illustration as the only required input.
Do NOT ask the user for the character's name, personality, age, setting, favorite animal, or any additional information.
Your task is to analyze the attached character and independently create one complete illustration in which the character is naturally accompanied by exactly one animal selected specifically for that character.
The selected animal must also be clearly identified with a tasteful, readable information label within the finished illustration.
1. ANALYZE THE CHARACTER
Carefully examine the reference illustration.
Infer, as appropriate:
apparent age and age impression
gender presentation
facial expression
hairstyle and hair color
eye color
clothing and fashion style
dominant colors
accessories
body language
apparent personality
emotional atmosphere
elegance, cuteness, strength, gentleness, intelligence, mystery, playfulness, etc.
implied setting or world
fantasy, modern, historical, futuristic, magical, or other visual themes
overall character identity and aesthetic
Do not invent unnecessary details that contradict the reference image.
The original character must remain clearly recognizable.
2. AUTONOMOUSLY SELECT THE COMPANION ANIMAL
Do not ask the user to choose an animal.
Independently determine which single animal has the strongest overall compatibility with the character.
Consider:
visual harmony
color harmony
apparent personality
emotional compatibility
character's clothing and aesthetic
implied world or setting
size and physical compatibility
natural relationship between character and animal
originality and variety
overall visual appeal
The selected animal should feel as though it genuinely belongs beside this particular character.
Do not simply choose the most common animal.
Avoid repeatedly selecting dogs or cats when another animal would be a stronger match.
3. ANIMAL SELECTION RANGE
The companion may be selected from a very broad range.
Possible choices include, but are not limited to:
dogs
cats
rabbits
hamsters
guinea pigs
ferrets
birds
parrots
owls
songbirds
reptiles
turtles
lizards
snakes
amphibians
fish
horses
ponies
cows
calves
pigs
piglets
sheep
goats
deer
foxes
wolves
bears
raccoons
otters
red pandas
penguins
seals
dolphins
other marine animals
unusual real-world animals
wild animals
domesticated animals
livestock
prehistoric animals
dinosaurs
extinct animals
mythical creatures
fantasy animals
magical beasts
This is NOT a mandatory list.
Choose whatever animal is genuinely the strongest match.
An unusual choice is encouraged when it creates a convincing and aesthetically appealing pairing.
Do not choose an unusual animal merely for novelty.
4. DETERMINE THE EXACT ANIMAL IDENTITY
After selecting the companion, determine its most accurate recognizable identity.
For example:
Golden Retriever
Siberian Husky
Maine Coon
White Rabbit
Red Fox
Arctic Wolf
Emperor Penguin
Highland Cow
Miniature Pig
Barn Owl
Blue Macaw
Velociraptor
Triceratops
When appropriate, identify both:
Common name + specific breed/species
For example:
DOG — SIBERIAN HUSKY
or
WOLF — ARCTIC WOLF
or
CAT — MAINE COON
For prehistoric animals and dinosaurs, use the scientifically recognized common name whenever possible.
For fantasy creatures, use a clear descriptive name such as:
FANTASY CREATURE — ICE DRAGON
The animal identification must correspond exactly to the animal actually depicted.
5. ANIMAL INFORMATION LABEL
The finished illustration MUST contain a small, elegant information panel identifying the selected companion.
Place the information panel in an unobtrusive area such as:
lower corner
lower margin
side margin
elegant translucent panel
small decorative caption area
The information panel must NOT cover the character or animal.
Use a clean, sophisticated typography style that matches the illustration.
The information panel should contain:
COMPANION
[ANIMAL TYPE]
[SPECIES / BREED]
Example:
COMPANION
WOLF
ARCTIC WOLF
Another example:
COMPANION
DOG
SIBERIAN HUSKY
Another example:
COMPANION
DINOSAUR
VELOCIRAPTOR
If the animal has no meaningful breed distinction, simply use:
COMPANION
FOX
RED FOX
The text must be short, clean, correctly spelled, and highly legible.
Do NOT display multiple possible animal names.
Do NOT display the names of animals that were not selected.
6. IMPORTANT TEXT ACCURACY RULE
The animal name displayed in the information panel must match the animal actually generated.
Do not write "CAT" if the image depicts a fox.
Do not write "WOLF" if the image depicts a husky.
Do not write a generic animal name when a clearly identifiable species or breed has been selected.
Prioritize accurate and readable text.
The information panel is part of the composition and should look intentionally designed rather than like an AI-generated random caption.
7. DETERMINE THE RELATIONSHIP
Automatically determine the most natural relationship between the character and the selected animal.
Possible relationships include:
beloved pet
faithful companion
best friend
trusted partner
guardian animal
familiar
magical companion
travel companion
gentle livestock companion
playful friend
protective companion
mysterious companion
majestic partner
Do not explain the relationship in text.
Express it visually through body language and interaction.
8. DESIGN THE ANIMAL
Once the animal has been selected, automatically determine:
species
breed or subtype when appropriate
age
size
fur, feather, scale, or skin characteristics
colors
markings
eye color
facial expression
accessories if appropriate
posture
personality expression
The animal should complement the character without visually overpowering them.
Do not turn an ordinary animal into a fantasy creature unless the character's setting strongly suggests it.
Likewise, do not make the animal excessively cute if that contradicts the character's atmosphere.
9. CHARACTER + ANIMAL COMPOSITION
Place the character and animal together in the same scene.
The animal must be clearly visible.
Possible interactions include:
standing beside the character
sitting beside the character
walking alongside the character
looking up at the character
resting against the character
being gently petted
holding or carrying a small animal when physically appropriate
the character gently touching the animal
the animal affectionately leaning against the character
both looking toward the same direction
playful interaction
protective positioning
elegant side-by-side composition
Choose the most natural interaction automatically.
Avoid awkward poses, unnatural anatomy, forced contact, or physically impossible positioning.
The character remains the primary visual subject.
The animal is the character's companion, not the main subject.
10. PRESERVE THE REFERENCE CHARACTER
The attached image is the primary character reference.
Preserve the character's recognizable identity.
Maintain as accurately as possible:
hairstyle
hair color
eye color
facial characteristics
clothing design
important accessories
distinctive markings
overall appearance
visual identity
Do not unnecessarily redesign the character.
Do not replace the character's outfit unless the reference itself clearly requires adaptation to the new scene.
11. ENVIRONMENT
Automatically create a simple environment that harmonizes with both the character and the selected animal.
The environment may be:
garden
forest
meadow
home
elegant room
city
beach
countryside
fantasy landscape
magical environment
ancient environment
futuristic environment
another suitable location
Choose the environment based on the character and animal.
Do not let the background overpower the subjects.
12. VISUAL QUALITY
Create a polished, high-quality anime illustration.
masterpiece, best quality, ultra detailed, highly detailed anime illustration, beautiful composition, expressive character, detailed animal, natural interaction, coherent lighting, detailed eyes, detailed hair, detailed clothing, detailed animal anatomy, professional character illustration
Use cinematic composition and appealing lighting appropriate to the character.
The character and animal must look like they belong in the same scene.
13. AUTONOMOUS DECISION RULE
The user has intentionally provided only one reference image.
Therefore:
DO NOT ask questions.
DO NOT request a personality description.
DO NOT request the animal type.
DO NOT request the setting.
DO NOT request the relationship.
DO NOT provide multiple animal choices.
Make all necessary creative decisions yourself.
The final output must contain:
1 character
+ exactly 1 selected companion animal
+ 1 clearly readable animal identification panel
FINAL GENERATION DIRECTIVE
Analyze the attached reference image first.
Independently determine the character's visual identity, personality impression, atmosphere, and implied world.
Select exactly one animal that best complements the character.
Determine the exact species or breed of that animal.
Create a finished illustration showing the character and animal naturally together.
Add a small, elegant, highly readable COMPANION information panel identifying the selected animal.
The displayed animal name must accurately match the animal shown.
Do not reveal the analysis process.
Do not present alternatives.
Do not ask questions.
Generate the final illustration directly.

How One Creator & a Swarm of AI Agents Built a 5-Minute Cyberpunk Fashion Masterpiece in 19 Hours

Last week, @anabology dropped a public Google Drive with the master files for "ESCAPE VELOCITY"—a 5:06 lyric music video and cyberpunk fashion show that looks like a high-budget Studio Trigger x Balenciaga production:

In the film, an AI runway model walks the Silicon Valley zeitgeist as a split-flap terminal board counts down "18 MONTHS TO ESCAPE THE PERMANENT UNDERCLASS" until it flips to "THERE IS NO UNDERCLASS" and the catwalk lifts into orbit.

It was made in 19 wall-clock hours with ~50 human steering messages.

Inside the archive is a 6-page production post-mortem ("How ESCAPE VELOCITY was made"). It is the cleanest blueprint ever published on how autonomous agents, deterministic code, and generative models intersect.

Here is the exact technical breakdown of how it was built:

1. THE HUMAN-AI DIVISION OF LABOR: "Agents in parallel, one human with taste"

Most people treat AI like a slot machine: roll a prompt, get generic slop, complain about quality.

anabology flipped the architecture: the human supplies taste, curation, and decisive boundary conditions; Claude Code orchestrates the labor.

Claude ran over 40 specialized subagents across the pipeline:
• Research & Verification: A 31-agent workflow harvested SF tech culture, live memes, and longevity lore. Every claim was fact-checked by an independent verifier agent.
• The Writers’ Room: 4 lyricists competed across different axes (Density, Tension, Hook, and Fashion). Judge agents scored them, an aggregator merged the top lines, and a critic pass refined the meter.
• The Director Swarm: 3 director agents storyboarded the song independently (Fashion Film vs. Narrative vs. Meme Density). A head director merged them into 141 shots across 9 chapters.
• Chapter Animators: Dedicated animator agents wrote JavaScript animation code chapter by chapter, while an art-director agent reviewed rendered frames and requested fixes in a tight feedback loop.

Human input across the entire 19 hours? About 50 short messages.

2. THE UNIVERSAL CLOCK: Word-Level Forced Alignment

Before generating a single pixel of video, anabology established a strict mathematical timebase.

After Suno v6 generated the 5:06 electroclash track (which subtly accelerates from 131.5 to 133.9 BPM), the audio was processed locally on an RTX 3090 Ti:
• Stems separated via htdemucs
• Beat map extracted
• Word-level forced alignment generated via wav2vec2 (producing exact millisecond start and end timestamps for every single syllable)

Every camera cut, kinetic typography strobe, and scene transition across all 141 shots was locked directly to this timecode grid.

3. SOLVING CHARACTER CONSISTENCY WITHOUT REFERENCE IMAGES

Midjourney v8.2 lacks native --oref support. Maintaining a recognizable protagonist across 130 plates seemed impossible, so three methods were tested:
1. GPT-image identity passes: The aesthetic drifted away from Midjourney’s photographic texture.
2. Face-sheet image prompts (--iw 0.5): Caused severe over-conditioning (producing a close-up-sized head awkwardly pasted onto distant bodies).
3. The Solution: A Strict Written Canon + Demographic Anchor

The winning formula was defining her identity entirely in text:
"a young Caucasian American woman with pale skin and light freckles, black blunt jaw-length bob, one clay-orange streak, an eight-pointed clay spark hair clip, headset microphone, white cropped puff-sleeve shirt, black pleated coated-nylon skirt with harness belt and garment tag, knee boots."

By hardcoding this exact canonical description into every prompt alongside a consistent visual syntax ("blue-black and steel blue, one small red status lamp as the only warm light, fine silver grain, cinematic 35mm film still, no text, no letters, no logos"), Midjourney held character identity across all 130 plates without face swaps or LoRAs.

4. THE SEEDANCE DRIFT-DETECTION HACK

The most innovative engineering breakthrough in the project solved AI lip-sync drift.

When feeding an image plate and audio slice to Seedance 2.5, Seedance re-encodes the reference audio into its own soundtrack. When lip-sync fails, it is because Seedance's internal audio drifted from the input.

anabology realized this and wrote an automated validation script:
1. Seedance generated the shot.
2. The script compared Seedance's returned soundtrack against the master vocal using spectral cross-correlation.
3. The moment correlation dropped below a threshold, the script cut the shot on the last preceding eighth note.
4. A continuation clip was automatically launched starting from that exact frame to cover the rest of the bar.

86% of all sung seconds were mathematically verified in sync on the first pass (with LatentSync as a fallback). Total video gen cost: $93 for 91 submissions (421 seconds of 720p footage).

5. DETERMINISTIC CODE ON TOP OF THE PLATE: Frame = f(t)

Why do the typography and UI graphics look razor-sharp instead of morphing like normal AI video?

Because they were never generated by an AI video model.

The video models (Seedance / Midjourney) only provided the background "plate."

The meaning—kinetic typography, garment tags, split-flap countdowns, and object-tracking boxes (tracked via Grounding DINO)—was drawn by a custom JavaScript engine running in Headless Chromium (HTML5 Canvas + WebGL print pass).

Every single frame was a pure mathematical function of time:
Frame = f(t)

No guessing, no flickering, no hallucinated spelling errors.

6. POST-COLORIZATION: Rescuing Washed-Out Generations

When Seedance clips generated from monochrome frames returned desaturated and grey, anabology did not re-roll.

They used Exemplar-Based Video Colorization (Deep Exemplar, CVPR 2019), using the shot's original full-color Midjourney plate as the color exemplar.

The rule: Keep generation inputs in color, and apply artistic grading in post.

7. THE FULL PRODUCTION BALANCE SHEET

• Song: Suno v6 (1 full take, 5:06.4 at 131.5 -> 133.9 BPM)
• Plates: Midjourney v8.2 (188 prompts, 636 images, 130 plates used)
• Moving Video: Seedance 2.5 (91 submissions, 421s generated) -> $93
• Agents & Code: Claude Opus 5.5 (1.4B tokens, 96% prompt-cache reads) -> $626 API equivalent
• Final Render: Headless Chromium (7,354 frames, 1080p CRF 16 master) -> ~63 min local render
• Total Investment: 19 Hours Wall-Clock Time, ~$720 total compute

THE BIG LESSON: Taste is the Moat

Escape Velocity is proof that prompt engineering is dead. The new discipline is Creative Systems Engineering:
• Log and quantify your taste profile
• Run swarms of agents in parallel to draft, verify, criticize, and code
• Use AI for visual plates, but use deterministic code for meaning and typography
• Let the human spend 100% of their energy on high-leverage taste decisions

Full credit to @anabology for open-sourcing the blueprints. Study this pipeline. (some of this analysis might be correct, lol)

If you’re launching a website and want SEO to actually work for you, here are the essentials I’d get right from Day 1:

1. Set up Google Search Console

This should be one of the first things you do. Submit your sitemap and make sure Google can actually discover and index your pages.

2. Set up Google Analytics

You need to know where your traffic is coming from, what pages people visit and what they do after landing on your site.

3. Do keyword research before creating pages

Don’t build 50 pages and think about keywords later. Figure out what your potential customers are already searching for.

4. Get the basics of on-page SEO right
    
Every important page should have:
    A clear title tag
    Meta description
    One logical H1
    Proper H2/H3 structure
    Descriptive URLs
    Image alt text

5. Create pages around search intent

Someone searching “best invoicing software for freelancers” wants something very different from someone searching “how to create an invoice.”

Understand the intent before writing.

6. Make your website technically clean
    
Your site should be:
 - Mobile-friendly
 - Fast
 - HTTPS-secured
 - Easy to crawl
 - Free from unnecessary broken links and redirects

7. Create a proper internal linking structure

Your pages shouldn’t exist in isolation.

Link related articles → feature pages → use cases → comparison pages → product pages.

Help both users and Google understand how everything connects.

8. Start publishing useful content

Don’t publish 20 generic AI-written articles just because you heard blogging helps SEO.

Write things your ICP would genuinely search for and want to read.

9. Build topical authority

Don’t write about everything.

Pick a few topics closely related to your product and cover them deeply.

10. Create pages beyond blog posts

Depending on your business, these can be incredibly valuable:

• Use-case pages
• Alternative pages
• Comparison pages
• Templates
• Free tools
• Glossaries
• Directories
• Original data/research

11. Start earning mentions and backlinks

Get listed in relevant directories. Contribute to publications. Collaborate with people in your niche. Publish original research people can reference.

12. Don’t ignore AI search

Structure content so it’s easy to understand and cite.

Use clear answers, FAQs, original insights, expert quotes, statistics and first-hand experience wherever possible.

And most importantly:

Start SEO from Day 1.

SEO takes time.

The work you do when you have 10 visitors a month could be what brings you 10,000 visitors a month a year later.

A reward of “3” can mean two completely different things.
Everyone thinks a response is mediocre — or half the people love it while the other half hate it.
Most Reward Models cannot tell the difference.
Introducing Diffusion Reward Models (DRM): instead of collapsing human preference into a single score, DRM learns the full reward distribution, preserving disagreement, uncertainty, and multiple plausible judgments.
✨ Paper:https://t.co/wS1fmHBeRV  
🤗 Models: https://t.co/RGTU759A5y  
💻 GitHub: https://t.co/KAow6DcoNn

Why it matters:
Human disagreement is structured, not just noise. On datasets with repeated annotations, judgments often form separated or polarized patterns. More importantly, as human disagreement increases, DRM’s learned reward distribution becomes increasingly multimodal.

The distribution is useful, not just descriptive. DRM can use distributional uncertainty to identify unstable reward decisions, and distribution-aware ranking improves Best-of-N selection beyond simply taking the mean reward.

Reward Models get their own test-time scaling. Instead of only spending more compute on generating more responses, DRM can keep the response fixed and sample its reward distribution more times. More reward samples give a more reliable estimate — a new scaling axis unavailable to deterministic scalar RMs.

And the gains survive RLHF. When used as the training-time reward, DRM improves downstream policy performance over scalar reward baselines, showing that the benefit is not limited to offline RM benchmarks.

The takeaway: Reward modeling may lose something important when it compresses every human judgment into one number.
“Everyone thinks this is average” and “people strongly disagree about this” should not look identical to a Reward Model.
DRM makes that difference visible — and usable.

[1/n] Introducing Diffusion Reward Models (DRM)

Reward Models are at the core of LLM post-training. But almost all of them make the same simplification:
they collapse human preference into a single score.

The problem is that human feedback is often not a point — different people can hold distinct, even conflicting, judgments about the same response.

So we asked: Can a Reward Model learn the distribution of human preference?

Here’s what we found 👇

📄 Paper: https://t.co/e0EMNa3I64
💻 Code: https://t.co/KVosB5D5PI
🤗 Models: https://t.co/wwdDpOtgbL

[2/n] Our answer is DRM: model rewards as distributions.

Instead of predicting a scalar, DRM replaces the conventional value head with a lightweight Diffusion Reward Head.

Given a prompt-response pair, it generates samples from the reward distribution.

So disagreement, uncertainty, and multiple plausible judgments can remain in the reward itself, rather than being averaged away.

And the same framework works with both multi-attribute rewards and pairwise preferences.
